summary.text: The proof’s decisive step is a structural contradiction for a smaller odd composite: a power-of-two totient forces every prime divisor to be of Fermat form \(p=2^{2^a}+1\), and totient factorization then expresses \(N\) as a sum of distinct \(2^a\)’s with \(a<N_{\mathrm{idx}}\), impossible because their total is \(<2^{N_{\mathrm{idx}}}=N\). The bounds \(\varphi(m)<m\) and \(\varphi(m)\le m/2\) for even \(m\) reduce any smaller candidate to that case (or to the Fermat number itself if prime), while direct totient formulas provide the relevant candidates.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler's totient function, and define
\[
a(n)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^n\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
We shall prove the slightly more general statement that, for every positive integer \(r\), if
\[
N=2^r,\qquad F_r=2^{2^r}+1=2^N+1,
\]
then
\[
a(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_r,&F_r\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F_r\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
Taking \(r=33\) gives exactly the claimed result.

We first record the number-theoretic facts needed in the proof.

**1. Basic totient facts.** For every \(t\geq 0\),
\[
\varphi(2^{t+1})=2^t.
\]
Indeed, among the integers modulo \(2^{t+1}\), exactly the odd ones are relatively prime to \(2^{t+1}\), and there are \(2^t\) of them.

Also, if \(m>1\), then
\[
\varphi(m)<m.
\]
If \(m\) is even, we have the sharper estimate
\[
\varphi(m)\leq \frac m2.
\]
For the latter inequality, every residue relatively prime to an even number \(m\) must be odd, and there are only \(m/2\) odd residue classes modulo \(m\).

For a positive integer \(m\), let \(S\) be the set of its distinct prime divisors. The usual product formula for the totient gives
\[
\varphi(m)
 =m\prod_{p\in S}\left(1-\frac1p\right)
 =\left(\prod_{p\in S}(p-1)\right)
   \left(\frac{m}{\prod_{p\in S}p}\right).
\tag{1}
\]
The second factor is an integer: if \(m=\prod_{p\in S}p^{e_p}\), then it is \(\prod_{p\in S}p^{e_p-1}\). In particular, if \(m\) is odd, this second factor is odd. Formula (1) also shows that, for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\),
\[
p-1\mid\varphi(m).
\tag{2}
\]

We shall repeatedly use the elementary fact that every divisor of a power of two is itself a power of two. We shall also use uniqueness of the decomposition of a positive integer into a power of two times an odd number: if \(Q\) is odd and
\[
2^A=2^B Q,
\]
then \(A=B\) and \(Q=1\). This follows immediately by comparing the exact powers of two dividing the two sides.

**2. Primes one more than a power of two.** We need the standard observation that if \(u>0\) and \(2^u+1\) is prime, then \(u\) itself is a power of two.

To prove this, write
\[
u=2^a d
\]
where \(d\) is odd. If \(d>1\), put \(x=2^{2^a}\). Since \(d\) is odd, \(x+1\) divides \(x^d+1\): explicitly,
\[
x^d+1=(x+1)(x^{d-1}-x^{d-2}+\cdots-x+1).
\]
Here \(x+1>1\), and because \(d>1\), it is strictly smaller than \(x^d+1=2^u+1\). Thus \(2^u+1\) would have a proper nontrivial divisor and could not be prime. Hence \(d=1\), so \(u=2^a\), as claimed.

It follows in particular that if \(m\) is odd, \(\varphi(m)\) is a power of two, and \(p\mid m\) is prime, then \(p\) is a Fermat prime. Indeed, by (2), \(p-1\) divides the power of two \(\varphi(m)\), so
\[
p-1=2^u
\]
for some \(u\geq0\). Because \(m\) is odd, \(p\neq2\), and therefore \(p>2\), so \(u>0\). As \(p=2^u+1\) is prime, the preceding paragraph gives \(u=2^a\) for some \(a\geq0\). Thus
\[
p=2^{2^a}+1,
\qquad p-1=2^{2^a}.
\tag{3}
\]

**3. The crucial odd-composite obstruction.** We now prove that if \(r>0\) and \(N=2^r\), there is no odd composite integer \(m\) satisfying
\[
\varphi(m)=2^N.
\tag{4}
\]

Suppose, for contradiction, that such an \(m\) exists, and let \(S\) be the set of its distinct prime divisors. By (3), for every \(p\in S\) there is a nonnegative integer \(a_p\) such that
\[
p-1=2^{2^{a_p}}.
\tag{5}
\]
The indices \(a_p\) are distinct for distinct primes \(p\). Indeed, equality \(a_p=a_q\) in (5) would give \(p-1=q-1\), and hence \(p=q\).

Set
\[
Q=\frac{m}{\prod_{p\in S}p}.
\]
Because \(m\) is odd, \(Q\) is odd. Substituting (5) into the totient formula (1) yields
\[
\varphi(m)
 =\left(\prod_{p\in S}2^{2^{a_p}}\right)Q
 =2^KQ,
\qquad
K=\sum_{p\in S}2^{a_p}.
\tag{6}
\]
Combining (4) and (6), we obtain
\[
2^N=2^KQ.
\]
Since \(Q\) is odd, uniqueness of the power-of-two times odd decomposition gives
\[
K=N\quad\text{and}\quad Q=1.
\tag{7}
\]

The equality \(Q=1\) says that every prime divisor of \(m\) occurs to exponent exactly one; that is, \(m\) is squarefree. Since \(m\) is composite, it must therefore have at least two distinct prime divisors, so \(S\) has at least two elements.

Now fix \(p\in S\). Because there is at least one other prime divisor, the sum defining \(K\) contains, besides \(2^{a_p}\), at least one further positive summand. Hence
\[
2^{a_p}<K=N=2^r.
\]
Powers of two are strictly increasing, so this implies
\[
a_p<r.
\tag{8}
\]
Thus the distinct indices \(a_p\) all belong to \(\{0,1,\ldots,r-1\}\). Consequently,
\[
K=\sum_{p\in S}2^{a_p}
 \leq \sum_{i=0}^{r-1}2^i
 =2^r-1
 <2^r=N.
\]
This contradicts \(K=N\) from (7). Therefore no odd composite \(m\) can satisfy (4).

We now determine \(a(N)\).

### Case 1: \(F_r\) is prime

Recall that \(F_r=2^N+1\). Since \(F_r\) is prime,
\[
\varphi(F_r)=F_r-1=2^N.
\]
Thus \(F_r\) is an admissible integer in the definition of \(a(N)\), and so
\[
a(N)\leq F_r.
\]

Conversely, let \(m>0\) be any admissible integer, so \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\). Since \(r>0\), we have \(N=2^r\geq2\), and hence \(2^N\geq4\). Therefore \(m\neq1\), because \(\varphi(1)=1\) is not divisible by \(2^N\). Thus \(m>1\), and \(\varphi(m)>0\). Divisibility then implies
\[
2^N\leq\varphi(m).
\]
Using \(\varphi(m)<m\), we get
\[
2^N<m,
\]
so, as \(m\) is an integer,
\[
m\geq2^N+1=F_r.
\]
Every admissible \(m\) is therefore at least \(F_r\), while \(F_r\) itself is admissible. Hence
\[
a(N)=F_r.
\]

### Case 2: \(F_r\) is not prime

First,
\[
\varphi(2^{N+1})=2^N,
\]
so \(2^{N+1}\) is admissible. Therefore
\[
a(N)\leq2^{N+1}.
\tag{9}
\]
It remains to show that no smaller positive integer is admissible.

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(m>0\) satisfies
\[
2^N\mid\varphi(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
m<2^{N+1}.
\tag{10}
\]
Again \(m\neq1\), since \(N\geq2\) and \(2^N\nmid1=\varphi(1)\). Hence \(m>1\), so \(0<\varphi(m)<m\). Because \(2^N\mid\varphi(m)\), there is a positive integer \(k\) such that
\[
\varphi(m)=2^Nk.
\]
But (10) gives
\[
2^Nk=\varphi(m)<m<2^{N+1}=2\cdot2^N.
\]
Thus \(0<k<2\), whence \(k=1\). We have proved
\[
\varphi(m)=2^N.
\tag{11}
\]

We next show that \(m\) must be odd. If \(m\) were even, the even-number totient estimate would give
\[
2^N=\varphi(m)\leq\frac m2.
\]
On the other hand, \(m<2^{N+1}\) implies \(m/2<2^N\), a contradiction. Hence \(m\) is odd.

There are now two possibilities.

* If \(m\) is prime, then (11) gives
  \[
  m-1=\varphi(m)=2^N,
  \]
  and hence
  \[
  m=2^N+1=F_r.
  \]
  This would make \(F_r\) prime, contrary to the assumption of this case.

* If \(m\) is composite, then \(m\) is an odd composite integer satisfying \(\varphi(m)=2^N\), where \(N=2^r\). This is impossible by the odd-composite obstruction proved above.

Both alternatives are impossible. Therefore no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(2^{N+1}\). Combining this lower bound with (9) yields
\[
a(N)=2^{N+1}.
\]

Finally take \(r=33\). Then
\[
N=2^{33},
\qquad
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=2^N+1.
\]
The general result gives
\[
\boxed{
a(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{2^{33}+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}}
\]
This is precisely the conjectured conditional value.
